thread.title: UPDATE: CVS joins the backlash against airbrushing

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: CVS joins the backlash against airbrushing
text:
By Quentin Fottrell, MarketWatch
Airbrushing apps promote worrying trends on Facebook and Instagram about what is considered beautiful
Millions of social media users strive to take the perfect selfie and yearn to hear those three little words. But can you even believe what you see anymore? CVS (CVS) said Monday that "it will not digitally alter or change a person's shape, size, proportion, skin or eye color or enhance or alter lines, wrinkles or other individual characteristics." It will put a "CVS Beauty Mark" label on images that have not been airbrushed or altered.
There's been backlash against photo editors who alter photos to conform to just one idea of what's considered beautiful in recent years (http://www.independent.co.uk/news/media/advertising/lor233al-ads-banned-over-airbrushing-2326477.html), but appears to have picked up steam with the women-led #MeToo movement. Last November, Academy Award-winning actress Lupita Nyong'o criticized Grazia magazine for airbrushing a cover photo of her. The magazine lightened her skin tone and removed some of her hair.
"Disappointed that Grazia U.K. edited out and smoothed my hair to fit a more Eurocentric notion of what beautiful hair looks like," Nyong'o tweeted to her 804,000 Twitter (TWTR) followers last month. An Le, a Vietnamese photographer who took the photo, responded: "I realize now what an incredibly monumental mistake I have made and I would like to take this time to apologize to Ms Nyong'o and everyone else that I did offend."
(https://twitter.com/Lupita_Nyongo/status/928815665862942720)
But more people are applying the methods of the advertising industry to their own lives. Who can blame them? Facebook and dating profiles appear to be echoing what users have been fed by magazines and television advertisements for years. The billion-dollar online dating industry report a surge in membership this time of year. False advertising, like charity, appears to start at home: More people are also using the airbrushing on themselves.
False advertising is frustrating and a profile on a dating site is, in essence, an advertisement of you, said Abby Rodman, a psychotherapist in Boston. Too much airbrushing causes problems. "If you're creating a 'false advertisement' of yourself online through airbrushing and other means, the only outcomes are frustration for you -- when your date isn't interested in the real you -- and annoyance for the other person who invested their time with a you who doesn't truly exist."
(https://twitter.com/jundy__/status/945860505008312320)
A smudge, smudge here and a smudge, smudge there have never been easier. Adobe Photoshop once charged hundreds of dollars. It now charges just $9.99 a month (https://www.adobe.com/creativecloud/plans.html) for its most basic package. It must compete with a slew of easy-to-use apps: MoreBeaute2 (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/morebeaute2/id347331305?mt=8), is free on Apple's (AAPL) iOS and suggests removing freckles from children's photos; BeautyPlus (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.commsource.beautyplus&hl=en), free on iOS and Android, actually advertises a skin lightening feature. Call it Facetune 2 (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/facetune-2/id1149994032?mt=8): Revenge of the nerds. Anyone can have abs -- online, at least. ABSmatic (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/absmatic/id548697174?mt=8) costs $1 on iOS.
Airbrushing and other photo-trickery, once the preserve of Hollywood studios, is available to anyone with a smartphone and the ability to smudge, and they are altering our perceptions of what is deemed "beautiful." In addition to the usual overly smudged faces -- that appear to be fooling no one -- and white teeth reminiscent of Hollywood's Golden Age, many promote Western and Caucasian features as the norm. There is no room for natural blemishes or aging with these apps.
"The stakes have just risen with higher expectations and deeper letdowns when your man takes off his shirt and his abs turn out to have been painted," said Fran Walfish, a Beverly Hills, Calif.-based psychotherapist. "This trend is in part responsible for increased anxiety and a mad rush into my psychotherapy office. In Hollywood esthetics and physical beauty are essential while the 'forever young' is ever present. Sadly, youth rules."
(https://twitter.com/GeminiGotham/status/945818804734562304)
And yet a little light retouching can go a long way for some job seekers. Frown lines, dark circles under the eyes could give the impression of being tired or stressed out, experts say, so freshening up pictures can give you an extra edge on the competition. The AARP Public Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C., nongovernmental organization and interest group with members who are 50 years of age or over, says age discrimination is rife for older job seekers (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/why-older-workers-shave-years-off-their-resume-2015-05-07).
But tell that to online daters who click on the "perfect" photo and then watch a real human being walk in the door of Starbucks (SBUX). "It's safe to say that people don't like to be misled," Rodman said. That applies to choosing a person on a dating site or cosmetics. "And no one likes a bait and switch," she said. "Yes, go ahead and post your best photos but also be honest. Because honesty is real and refreshing, and -- unlike setting the unrealistic expectation of physical perfection -- it's a healthier foundation for any relationship."
-Quentin Fottrell; 415-439-6400; AskNewswires@dowjones.com
